verbatim_narration: Anthropic's IPO filing reported an eighty-point-seven-billion-dollar GAAP net loss for the first half of twenty twenty-six. That same day, financiers announced sixty-three billion dollars of equipment funding. A special vehicle would buy Broadcom hardware and lease it to Anthropic. That's not cash deposited into Anthropic's account. It's financing for machines customers may need later.

Anthropic disclosed about one hundred twenty-five-point-two billion dollars in rent under one five-year Broadcom equipment lease, excluding interest. On IPO filing day, financiers announced sixty-three billion dollars of equipment funding. One number describes rent; the other, financing. The public disclosures don't resolve their exact overlap. Adding them as independent debts would mislead investors.

Anthropic's reported net loss was eighty-point-seven billion dollars in the first half of twenty twenty-six. Its operating loss was about six hundred ninety-three million. Much of the difference reflects financial-instrument valuations, including a seventy-two-point-four-billion-dollar charge. That isn't eighty billion in cash spent running Claude. Future equipment commitments are a separate bet.

If Anthropic's proposed IPO closes, a company formed by its seven founders would hold one Class F share carrying fifty-point-one percent of votes on general shareholder matters—not half the equity. Separately, a long-term benefit trust would have special rights to select most directors, subject to contractual conditions. Public investors wouldn't automatically control either.
